title: Least squares by walking downhill
summary: f(x) = ½‖Ax − b‖² is a bowl: its gradient is Aᵀ(Ax − b), zero gradient is the normal equations, and AᵀA sets the step size.

blocks.title: The error at the start

define.meaning: Half the squared error of the fit $Ax$ to the data $b$: the least-squares objective. The $\frac12$ changes nothing about where the minimum is; it only makes the gradient tidier.

blocks.why: You have minimised $\|Ax - b\|^2$ by solving. Now the same bowl, walked down instead. First, how high up the walk starts.
blocks.prompt: $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$, $b = (2, 1, 2)$, and the start is $x_0 = (1, 0)$. Compute $f(x_0) = \frac12\|Ax_0 - b\|^2$.

slips.say: That is $\|Ax_0 - b\|^2$. This course's $f$ has a $\frac12$ in front.
That is $\frac12\|b\|^2$, the error at $x = (0, 0)$. Start from $Ax_0$ with $x_0 = (1, 0)$.

hints: $Ax_0$ is the first column of $A$, because $x_0 = (1, 0)$.

check.say: It must be at least $f$ at the best fit. You will meet that value at the end of the lesson.

blocks.title: The gradient of ½‖Ax − b‖²

define.meaning: The gradient of $\frac12\|Ax - b\|^2$. With the residual $r = b - Ax$ from least squares, it is $-A^\mathsf{T}r$: the residual hit with $A^\mathsf{T}$, with a minus sign.

blocks.why: This is the gradient every least-squares model is trained with. The sign is the trap: $A^\mathsf{T}(b - Ax)$ points uphill.

slips.say: That is $A^\mathsf{T}(b - Ax_0) = A^\mathsf{T}r$, minus the gradient. The sign matters here: with it, a step would go uphill.
That is the gradient of $\|Ax - b\|^2$ without the $\frac12$, which is twice as big. This course's $f$ has the $\frac12$.
Those are the first two entries of $Ax_0 - b$. Now multiply by $A^\mathsf{T}$: entry $i$ is column $i$ of $A$ dotted with $Ax_0 - b$.

hints: First $Ax_0 - b$, then each entry of the answer is a column of $A$ dotted with it.

check.say: Both entries negative means increasing either unknown lowers the error. At $x_0 = (1, 0)$ the fit is too low everywhere, so that should be so.

blocks.solution: $\nabla f(x_0) = (-1, -2)$. Downhill, $-\nabla f = (1, 2) = A^\mathsf{T}r$: the residual, sent back through $A^\mathsf{T}$, says how to change $x$.

blocks.title: One step towards the best fit
blocks.why: The update is the same as on every bowl so far. Only the gradient came from data.
blocks.prompt: With $\eta = \frac14$, step from $x_0 = (1, 0)$ using $\nabla f(x_0) = (-1, -2)$. Find $x_1$.

widget.name: descent-path
widget.caption: The bowl of $\frac12\|Ax - b\|^2$ over $x = (c, m)$. Work it out, then take a step.

slips.say: That adds $\eta\nabla f$. Subtract it: two minus signs make a plus here.
That subtracts the whole gradient. Multiply it by $\eta = \frac14$ first.

hints: $\eta\,\nabla f(x_0) = \frac14(-1, -2)$, and subtracting a negative adds.

check.say: $f(x_1)$ should be below $f(x_0) = \frac52$. That is the next screen.

blocks.title: The error fell
blocks.why: A step that does not lower the error is a bad step. Check this one.

check.say: It should be below $\frac52$, and above the best fit's error.

blocks.solution: $\frac{27}{16} \approx 1.69$, down from 2.5. The next step gives $\frac{405}{256} \approx 1.58$, and so on towards the bottom.

blocks.title: Where the walk stops
blocks.why: Gradient descent stops moving where the gradient is zero. That turns out to be an old friend.
blocks.prompt: Why the point where gradient descent on $f(x) = \frac12\|Ax - b\|^2$ stops is the least-squares solution. Put the lines in order. The first is given.

items.text: The steps stop changing $x$ exactly when $\eta\,\nabla f(x) = 0$.
Move $A^\mathsf{T}b$ across: $A^\mathsf{T}Ax = A^\mathsf{T}b$, the normal equations.

say.zero: This divides out $\eta$. Is the line with $\eta$ in it above?
say.formula: This writes out a gradient that is zero. Is the line saying it is zero above?
say.expand: This multiplies out a bracket. Which line has the bracket?
say.normal: This moves a term across. Is the line with both terms on one side above?

blocks.hint: Start from the step rule and follow it until it looks like something from least squares.
blocks.solution: Zero gradient is the normal equations, and $A^\mathsf{T}(Ax - b) = 0$ is your old "the residual is perpendicular to every column". Walking downhill and solving find the same point.

blocks.title: The destination
blocks.why: Solve for the point the walk is heading to, so you can see the iterates closing in on it.
blocks.prompt: Solve the normal equations $A^\mathsf{T}Ax = A^\mathsf{T}b$ for $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $b = (2, 1, 2)$.

slips.say: That divides $A^\mathsf{T}b = (3, 3)$ by the diagonal, 2. $A^\mathsf{T}A$ has off-diagonal 1s too: $2x + y = 3$ and $x + 2y = 3$.

hints: $2x + y = 3$ and $x + 2y = 3$: subtract them to see $x = y$.

check.say: The residual $r = b - Ax$ should be perpendicular to both columns of $A$: $r \cdot (1, 1, 0) = 0$ and $r \cdot (0, 1, 1) = 0$.

blocks.solution: $x^* = (1, 1)$, with $r = (1, -1, 1)$ and $f(x^*) = \frac32$. The iterates $(1, 0)$, $(\frac54, \frac12)$, $(\frac54, \frac{11}{16})$, … head there.
blocks.next: How big may the steps be?

blocks.title: The step limit from AᵀA

define.meaning: The matrix of second partial derivatives of $f$: the curvature in every direction. For $f = \frac12\|Ax - b\|^2$ it is $A^\mathsf{T}A$, so this bowl is the $\frac12 x^\mathsf{T}Hx$ of the last lesson with $H = A^\mathsf{T}A$.

blocks.why: The step-size rule from the bowls applies to least squares through $A^\mathsf{T}A$, whose eigenvalues are the squared singular values of $A$.
blocks.prompt: Gradient descent on $\frac12\|Ax - b\|^2$ converges when $0 < \eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}$, with $\lambda_{\max}$ the largest eigenvalue of $A^\mathsf{T}A = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$. What is the limit $2/\lambda_{\max}$?

slips.say: That uses the smallest eigenvalue, 1. The largest one sets the limit.
That divides by the largest singular value of $A$, $\sqrt3$. The curvature is its square, the eigenvalue of $A^\mathsf{T}A$: 3.
That divides by the diagonal entry 2. Use the largest eigenvalue of $A^\mathsf{T}A$.

hints: Find the eigenvalues of $A^\mathsf{T}A$: trace and determinant.

check.say: In the picture, slide $\eta$ just below and just above your limit and watch the path.

blocks.solution: $\eta < \frac23$. Here $\kappa = 3/1 = 3$, so the walk is quick; a nearly dependent pair of columns would make $\lambda_{\min}$ tiny and $\kappa$ huge, and the walk would crawl.

blocks.title: Why walk when you can solve?
blocks.body: With a million unknowns, $A^\mathsf{T}A$ has a million million entries and solving with it is out of reach. A gradient step needs only products with $A$ and $A^\mathsf{T}$, and machine learning goes further: each step uses the gradient from a small random batch of rows (stochastic gradient descent).

widget.caption: Your least-squares walk, 20 steps, ending at $(1, 1)$, the fit you would get by solving.

sideQuest.title: Walk to the least-squares fit, in numpy
sideQuest.body:
Only if you want to.

```
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [1.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]])
b = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 2.0])
x, eta = np.array([1.0, 0.0]), 1 / 4
for k in range(30):
    x = x - eta * A.T @ (A @ x - b)
print(x)                              # close to [1, 1]
print(np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0])  # [1, 1]
```
